items.text: Baan Noi charges about 22 dollars a head, which feels fair considering what you get. Order the pad see ew. It's got proper texture and the noodles actually taste like something. Don't bother with the green curry, they load it up with sugar and it ends up really cloying. That wasn't the only thing that dragged the meal down. We went in on Friday and the wait was long. It's clear the kitchen was in over its head. You can get a decent meal going here, but you have to put up with slow service. And I think you can get similar results at a bunch of other places around town. Getting the bad is too easy and the good is just too easy elsewhere. I'd rather eat somewhere that gets both right.

fellow travelers or anyone planning to see O and it's on hiatus. we booked la reve instead. we were staying at encore so theater was just a short walk away. we had seats in like the third row. i knew la reve gets compared to O, maybe even considered a copy of it so i thought it'd be a decent swap. it's not O, but pretty solid. does la reve have a story? maybe, but i didn't get it and didn't mind it. there's a performer who's like a lizard guy in a pool, floats still for a long time looking like a statue then goes and sneaks on people in the front rows, sprays them. the main show is the spectacle. they have the pool, moving platforms and stuff like swimmers and dives and walking on water. big dive from 25 feet. if you want a good show in vegas without cirque's insane prices this is a good swap. we left pretty impressed.

A rain gauge is pretty basic. You just catch rain with this fixed size hole. It channels the water down through a small tube that has depth marks on it. mm or inches, so you get the reading. The reading is basically the depth the rain would be if it all fell and just stayed on the ground no running off no soak in.
So the top hole usually is bigger than the tube to get it down to a smaller column. But they calibrate the scale to the area ratio, so still the right depth.
The two big problems I see are placement and evap. If you put it next to trees or buildings or fences you'll either get too little or too much depending on if it shelters or the run off and splash will add.
And the issue is evap, if you do not read it very soon, you'll be low.

On Thursdays, Marguerite always found the book in its fixed spot. Between the flour bins and the cooling racks, wedged against the wall. A Field Guide to Coastal Birds, spine cracked and faded, an old library stamp inside the cover, due date long past. 11 Thursdays she went. She checked the locks, checked with the day staff, and once she stayed late in the bakery with a thermos and a rolling pin. Nothing. The book just appeared between two and four in the morning. She never caught it in the moment.

Tonight it was heavier. She opened it up. A folded square of receipt paper had dropped out. It had a note written on it: *I keep meaning to bring it back to the library, but I walk past your window on the way, and the light is on, and I think, somebody's awake. Then I leave it here instead. Sorry. I'll stop if you ask me to.*
She read it twice. Behind her, the ovens were ticking and the first tray of rye bread was under its cloths.
She turned the receipt over and went hunting for a pencil, which was behind her ear. On the back she wrote: *Don't stop.* Then she tucked the paper back inside the cover, put the book on the front windowsill, and left the light on.

Its spine was flush with the steel edge. The same situation as the other Thursdays. He pulled it free, the cover was stuck with a square of blue prescription notepad. In ball point ink it said "The baker in chapter five reminds me of you. Thank you for keeping the lights on." He traced the deep indentation from the pen. The compressor shudder was the only sound. From the back, a slip of paper, due date card, yellowing, stamped in faded red ink, three days overdue. He walked over to the prep table, wrapped a warm glaze mapped cinnamon roll up in parchment paper, and put it in his coat pocket with the book.

4 stars. Keeping it. The space bar rattles. If you hit it with your thumb you get this clack clack, like a loose pen cap in a drawer. E repeats sometimes, like the word example becomes eexample and I have to backspace. Happens maybe once an afternoon. Always when I type fast and not looking. I paid $38. Keeping it anyway because of the switches, I asked the seller what the switches are, took them a week to respond. But I pried a keycap off to see what they were, brown tactiles, little bump under your finger and soft bottom out. Old membrane board feels like pressing wet cardboard, compared to this. My job is mostly email, 2-3 hours at a time. Wrists don't hurt when I finish. That mattered more than the rattle. Returning it would have meant paying postage and boxing it and waiting, not having a keyboard while waiting. Stays on desk, I put spacebar tap more towards middle now.

Two years ago I called Rockmount Ranch Wear for two shirts for my dad. They never turned up because the rep botched the address, wrote 7 by hand and they read it as a 1. So ours was 5407 but the shirts went to 5401. The folks at 5401 took the box to the UPS store for a return. Just disappeared. Never saw or heard of them again. It was several weeks later before we found out. We ordered another two shirts while the thing was unresolved. Rockmount wouldn't refund the first pair, that was in the midst of our dispute. At that stage the owner came in and handled it himself. He said the shipment went to the wrong address but we wouldn't get refund until they were returned. Said our bad behavior was part of the reason, we weren't friendly to the 5401 folks who were just four doors away. We argued chargeback with credit-card company and eventually got a credit.

So if you're flying Turkish, just a heads up. I had Harbin to Beijing domestic, then their Beijing to Istanbul. Harbin leg got delayed, I missed the connection. Go to the Turkish counter no one would take responsibility or rebook me. I slept at the airport. In morning asked for a ticket, they said flights overbooked, could take days to get me to Istanbul unless I pay for business. But I had to get there, so accepted it. Still furious and honestly in disbelief at Turkish.

So every Thursday around 2pm, in the milk crate by the backdoor, Imre finds something in it that is not milk, something else. First week, its a Field Guide to Mushrooms of the Northeast, has the Carver Street Library stamp on the flyleaf, due date long past. Second week, same book. Third week, same. He stopped reshelving it in his head. It lives on the flour bench now, between the scale and the rye starter tub, cover gone soft with dough dusted thumbprints. Tonight, he slid the crate out with his hip, hands still in oven mitts, and the book was there again, heavier than usual. A square of yellow paper stuck out near page 112. He peeled the mitts off. The note was in pencil, small, slanted hard right. It said, your door smells better than the library. I keep meaning to bring it to the right place. Is the morel on this page the one you use? T. Imre looked at the page. Nothing circled, morel sat there, wrinkled brown. He took the pencil from behind his ear, flipped the note, wrote: No. Never used one. Then after a moment, he added: Come at five, there's bread. Pressed it back in.

3:17 am, I hear the walk-in cooler kick in, proofing cabinet is humming. Slid the first loaves in the oven. The worn paperback is back again, sitting in the wicker basket by the back door, The Borrowers. For six Thursdays someone has left it here instead of the library two blocks over. The checkout card on the back is blank, just a barcode and a coffee ring on it. On pages 84 and 85 there was a folded note wedged in there. I wiped my hands on my apron and read it, it says "I can't get to the library before it closes. Please keep it here another week. I like knowing it's warm." I looked at the basket then at the cinnamon rolls cooling off on the rack. Grabbed the one with the most icing, wrapped it in wax paper, slipped the note back in the book, and set both by the door. 4:50 I pulled the loaves, knocked them out of their pans and put the next tray in.

I payed 38 dollars for this second hand mechanical keyboard, so I hope was modest: no missing keycaps, no sticky mystery grime, and switches that didn't feel like gravel. And on that scale it did fine. It arrived clean enough to just place on my desk and use without doing a full clean. The keys have a pleasant weight to them. The board is comfortable, and I type a lot of long emails and it's fine. My fingers don't feel beat up after long stretches, which is more than some cheap new boards.
The rough edges aren't hidden. The spacebar rattle when I hit it off center, clacks loose and cheap sounding. And one key repeat every now and then. Ill look up to see extra letters in a sentence. Not constant, but irritating.
The communication was the weak point. I asked what switches it had, and the reply was a week later, and by the time I checked for myself. I wanted to return it. But then I pictured packing and paying shipping. So for 38 dollars I kept it. It's flawed but it works.

I’ve been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life, the under-21 version of it. So I’ve sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at Wynn, we finally saw that one, and honestly it’s mixed, maybe worse than mixed. The good is the circular stage is genuinely smart. You look down into it, so from any seat you get a good view, and its a rare thing in Vegas. Some acts are good, strength stuff, aerialists, divers, all the good stuff. They are athletes, no question. But it reminds me of Cirque du Soleil, just not in a rip-off way, just that you see comparable feats done with maybe more clarity. But clarity is the problem. I still dont know what’s the story is about? Dream? Guy? Water? Its pretty images thrown at you with no real idea of what it was trying to tell. And its just too much going on. Too many things, too many people, too many wow moments on top of each other. More restraint would be nice. This is just more is better, stereotypical Vegas spectacle, so they crammed all in, and more is better, but not for us. Ticket: staying Wynn or Encore, they have deal where instead of 125 for the show you pay 99, that’s a good deal. Would I see it again, probably not, and pay again, no. Apart from a few stunts it was average, not blown away. I think nobody was. Some friends of mine liked it, so if you’ve not seen it, it’s probably worth a watch, just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

Picked up a second-hand mechanical keyboard, used, thirty eight bucks. Didn’t expect perfection and got pretty much that. Came over clean enough, worked out of the box, nice relief honestly. Typing feel is better than I expected for the money. I write long emails for work, keys are fine, hands don’t get tired after a couple of hours on them.

Some issues. Spacebar rattles, worst at the edges, cheapens the whole board when you strike it. Also one key does this stutter thing, repeats occasionally, drives me nuts when I’m hammering it out and then have to go back and delete the extra letter. Not constantly but often enough to mention. Did ask seller about the switches, he only answered after a week, kinda figured it out on my own by then. Thought about returning it but at $38, return shipping is not worth the effort. Kept it because works and comfortable, not perfect.

Rye, at 3:40 in the morning, while it was proofing. I found it again and again, the library book, that one next to the flour bin by the back door. The plastic was cold from the alley. Fourth Thursday in a row that this has happened. Same book. A Field Guide to Night Birds, Eastgate Branch, and there was a new due date slip every time. And I was dropping it in the return box on my way home every single week and then next Thursday some one pulled it out again and brought it back to me. Scraped off the dough from my knuckles and opened it up. And on the page about barn owls, someone had written a check mark next to the description, a long harsh scream. There was an index card folded out of the page. It said, you leave the vent fan on. The alley smells like bread until five in the morning. At three-thirty, I walk my mom's dog because she can't anymore. Heard one of these behind the dumpster. I keep checking out this book again. So she read that twice while the oven timer ticked down and outside, the fan was blowing steam across the wet dumpster lid. Flipped it over and with the grease pencil, the one that we mark the trays with. I wrote, rye's out at 4:15. Then I took a heel from yesterday's loaf and wrapped it in wax paper, put it on the outside step. And set the book on top of it, left the back door open a couple of inches, like an inch.

So we came in at 7:20 on Sunday. This is a hotel buffet. We wanted to make sure we had enough time before the show upstairs at 10pm. We got into the digital waitlist - a total useless system. At 8:23pm they sent us back to pay. At 8:40pm we got told that probably not until 9:15pm we would get a table. So it was our party of two. No solution. Management should have warned us first. That we were not going to get a table until long after the pay time. That would have saved hours of wasted time. Total failure. If I gave one star to the food, I would give zero to the service. Not sure if zero stars is an option but that is what I would give.

The freezer is the problem here. Out long enough to eat into the 12,400 meals you banked. Fixing it takes the whole $7,500, then it goes, then the group can keep going at the current pace. If that money doesn't come in the next month you're in for turning away some of the walk in traffic. The drivers are there, the demand is obviously there. The numbers for spring show you're capable of 2,600 more meals this quarter, and the new 3 drivers can hit outlying routes the old crew couldn't, and that's the change in the numbers. The equipment getting fixed is the only thing left.

Picked this keyboard up used for 38. Knew 38 doesn't get you a pristine board, didn't get one. Spacebar rattles on a lot of presses, not every, but I catch it in the silence right before I start writing out a sentence. One key ghosts randomly, type a word it comes out doubled, so just reread everything before I hit send. That habit has saved me from a few mistakes but honestly wish I had to learn it on my own, not the board that forced me. Asked the seller what switches are on here, got answer week later, by then I'd already taken it, figured out feel on my own, so whatever. Keeping it mostly because it's comfortable enough to use, I write emails long enough that I stop noticing my hands on it and they don't tire out after an hour. Switches have a weight, a feel that's nice. Considered returning it, but the rattle isn't bothering me that bad, it's not bad enough, just the fact of having to deal with the return, that's a hassle, so here it stays.
